## Why a Write-Through Cache Can Still Serve Stale Reads

A write-through cache forwards every write to the backing store before acknowledging it, so the backing store is never behind the cache. This is often taken to mean reads through the cache are always fresh. They are not: write-through guarantees the order in which *this* cache's writes reach the store, not that every read path observes the same latest value.

The main mechanism is the write acknowledgment. Many designs acknowledge the write once the store has accepted it, not once it is globally visible. If the store is a replicated or quorum system, a write can be durable on one replica while another replica still answers reads with the old value. A second cache instance, or a reader that reaches the store directly, can therefore return a value older than one already acknowledged.

Multiple writers compound this. Two caches fronting the same store, each write-through, can interleave: cache A writes v2 to the store, cache B holds v1 in its own lines, and a read through B returns v1 after v2 was acknowledged. Write-through says nothing about invalidating other caches' copies.

Finally, a read can be raced by a concurrent write. Even single-cache designs typically service reads from cache while the write is in flight to the store; the read completes with the pre-write value. This is linearizable only if reads and writes are serialized, which a simple write-through cache does not do.

The fix is not to switch to write-back; it is to make visibility explicit: invalidate all cache copies on write, read through a single ordered path, or attach versions to values and have readers reject older ones. Write-through alone gives no read-consistency guarantee.

## Risks

1. Assuming store acknowledgment equals global visibility, so readers on other replicas or caches return superseded values.
2. Multiple write-through caches fronting one store without cross-cache invalidation, letting a read through one cache return a value another cache has already overwritten.
3. Reads serviced from cache while a write is in flight, returning the pre-write value even in a single-cache design.
